512.title: Ki Tavo: first fruits (Deuteronomy 26:1–11)
512.hook: the farmer brings the first fruits in a basket and tells his people's story
512.howItsDone: Bikkurim were brought to the Temple between Shavuot and Sukkot. They have not been brought since the Temple's destruction, but verses from the farmer's declaration in Deuteronomy 26 (26:5–8) are expounded line by line in the Passover Haggadah, and Shavuot is still called the festival of first fruits.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amalek and the weary at the back of the line. Your line was watch the stragglers. Did you notice who was trailing behind? Today, a new portion, Ki Tavo: when you come in. Day five hundred twelve.

A farmer in the hills walks out into his field early in the season and sees it: the first fig of the year, swelling on the branch. He doesn't pick it and eat it. He ties a reed around it, a little marker that says this one is set aside. Weeks later he carries it, with the first barley and grapes and olives, in a basket, up the road to Jerusalem. The Mishnah describes the procession: an ox with gilded horns, a flute playing in front, whole villages walking together. Today: the first fruits, and the speech the farmer has to make when he arrives.
screen: `A FIG WITH A REED TIED ON.` → `A BASKET ON THE ROAD UP.` → `A FLUTE, AN OX, A VILLAGE.`

segments.voice: The word is bikkurim. First fruits. It comes from the same Hebrew root as bechor, firstborn. The instruction in Deuteronomy twenty-six is simple. When you come into the land and settle it, take some of the first of every fruit, put it in a basket, bring it to the place God chooses, and hand it to the priest. Later tradition limited the offering to the seven kinds the land is praised for: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates. But the surprising part isn't the fruit. It's the speech. The farmer doesn't say, look what I grew. He tells history: a wandering ancestor, slavery in Egypt, a cry, a rescue, a land. Only then does he set the basket down. Tomorrow we'll open that speech line by line. The Mishnah adds a detail that's easy to miss. At first, people who could read the Hebrew recited it themselves, and those who couldn't were prompted. The ones who needed help were embarrassed, and some stopped coming. So the rule changed: the priest read it for everyone, and everyone repeated after him, the scholar and the farmer who never learned to read, the same words at the same pace. And the passage ends with joy: rejoice in all the good you've been given, you and your household, the Levite, and the stranger in your midst. The first doesn't go into storage, or straight into your own mouth. The first goes to thanks, and the thanks is shared.
screen: `BIKKURIM: THE FIRST OF THE FRUIT.` · `NOT A BRAG: A STORY.` · `EVERYONE REPEATS AFTER THE PRIEST.` · `REJOICE, WITH THE STRANGER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST GOES TO THANKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give the first of something. Settle, and breathe. Think about what comes first in your day. The first cup of coffee, the first hour, the first money of the month, the first good news you'll want to share. Pick one. Before you use it on yourself, imagine tying a reed around it. This one is marked. Maybe the first sip comes with a moment of thanks. Maybe the first ten minutes of the morning go to someone else. Decide what your first will be, and who or what it goes to. The bell holds the time.
Bikkurim. First fruits, from the root for firstborn. Carried up in a basket, and set down with a story.
Your line: the first goes to thanks. Today, before you enjoy the first of something, pause for one breath of thanks, or pass a piece of it on. Day five hundred twelve.

513.title: Ki Tavo: a wandering Aramean (Deuteronomy 26:5)
513.hook: "A wandering Aramean was my father", now at the heart of the Passover Haggadah
513.howItsDone: Deuteronomy 26:5–8 is the core text of the Maggid section of the Passover Haggadah, where it is read and expounded phrase by phrase, opening with the Haggadah's reading of 'arami oved avi'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bikkurim, the first fruits in a basket. Your line was the first goes to thanks. What was your first, and where did it go? Today, the story the farmer tells as he sets the basket down. Day five hundred thirteen.

At the Passover seder, the Haggadah reaches a long stretch of verses and commentary, the telling of the Exodus itself. Look closely at the verses it's built on, and they aren't from the book of Exodus. They're from Deuteronomy, from the speech of the farmer with his basket. The Haggadah takes his few lines and reads them slowly, phrase by phrase, as the backbone of the night's story. And it starts with a phrase readers still argue over.
screen: `THE SEDER TABLE.` → `NOT EXODUS: DEUTERONOMY.` → `THE FARMER'S SPEECH.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, the speech begins: "A wandering Aramean was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there, few in number; and he became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous." In Hebrew, arami oved avi. Three words, and readers don't agree on what they say. Oved can mean wandering, lost, or perishing. Commentators like Ibn Ezra and Rashbam read it plainly: my ancestor, Jacob, or perhaps Abraham, was a wandering Aramean, a man without land of his own. The Haggadah, and Rashi after it, read it another way: an Aramean, Laban, tried to destroy my father Jacob. Two readings, both kept. One says, we came from wanderers. The other says, we came through danger. Now notice what the farmer is doing. He's standing with his own harvest, settled at last, and the first thing out of his mouth is: we were not always settled. My people were strangers once. And he says my father, not their father. It's personal. The Mishnah asks the same of everyone at the seder: begin with the shame and end with the praise, and tell it as your own story. Settled people are asked to remember, out loud, that they weren't always. The Torah ties that memory to its law: love the stranger, it says elsewhere, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. One line of family history, and a rule for how to treat the newcomer next door.
screen: `ARAMI OVED AVI.` · `WANDERING, OR PERISHING?` · `TWO READINGS, BOTH KEPT.` · `MY FATHER, NOT THEIR FATHER.` · then, large: `A WANDERING FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell your family's story in one line. Settle, and breathe. Go back as far as you know. A grandparent, a great-grandmother, a name on an old document, or just a guess. Where did they come from? What did they carry, or leave behind? Now try to say it in one sentence, the way the farmer does. Something like: my grandmother crossed an ocean with one suitcase. If you don't know your family's story, that not-knowing is part of many families' story too. Hold the line you've found, and let it sit. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. The portion that begins with arriving, and asks you to remember wandering.
Your line: a wandering father. Today, tell someone one line of your family's story, or ask someone for theirs. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: Ki Tavo: this day (Deuteronomy 26:16, 27:9)
514.hook: Rashi: let the commandments feel new each day, as if given today
514.tomorrow: Ki Tavo: coming in, going out (Deuteronomy 28:3–6)
514.howItsDone: Rashi's reading of 'this day' is often taught as the reason a daily prayer or weekly Torah portion should not become routine; many teachers ask students to find something new in a familiar text each time it comes around.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farmer's story: arami oved avi. Your line was a wandering father. Did you hear, or tell, one line of family history? Today, two small words Moses keeps repeating. Day five hundred fourteen.

Remember the last time something was new. A phone with the plastic still on the screen. The first day at a job, when you noticed every hallway. A friendship in its first weeks, when every message felt important. Now picture that same thing a year later. The phone is scratched. The hallways are invisible. The messages are routine. Nothing changed but your eyes. Moses is speaking to a people who have lived with God's commandments for forty years. And he keeps calling it today.
screen: `THE PLASTIC ON THE SCREEN.` → `A YEAR LATER: INVISIBLE.` → `FORTY YEARS, AND CALLED TODAY.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy twenty-six, verse sixteen: "This day the LORD thy God commandeth thee to do these statutes and ordinances." This day. But many of these laws had been given at Sinai, long before. A chapter later, Moses and the priests say: "Keep silence, and hear, O Israel; this day thou art become a people unto the LORD thy God." This day? They'd been a people for four decades. In Hebrew, the word is hayom: today. Rashi, the great eleventh-century commentator from France, reads it as an instruction about how to hold something old. On the first verse he says, in effect: every day these commandments should be in your eyes as new, as though you'd been commanded them that very day. On the second: each day, see yourself as if you had entered the covenant today. It's a teaching about attention. The danger in a long practice usually isn't rebellion. It's autopilot. The prayer you can say without hearing it. The blessing muttered on the way to the first bite. The person across the table you've stopped really seeing. Notice that Rashi doesn't say pretend it's new. He says let it be new in your eyes. The text stays the same. The eyes are the part that can change. Jewish life is full of repetition built on this hope: the same prayers every morning, the same Torah read every year, and an expectation that this time something in them will catch you differently. Hayom. Not a date on a calendar. A way of looking.
screen: `HAYOM: THIS DAY.` · `FORTY YEARS OLD, CALLED TODAY.` · `RASHI: NEW IN YOUR EYES.` · `THE TEXT STAYS; THE EYES CHANGE.` · then, large: `THIS DAY, NEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat one old practice as new. Settle, and breathe. Choose something you do so often you've stopped noticing it. A blessing, a greeting, the way you make tea, the walk to the front door, saying goodnight to someone. Walk through it slowly in your mind, as if for the first time. What would a stranger notice? What would you see if you'd never done it before? Find one detail you'd stopped seeing. Later today, do the thing for real, with that detail in view. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. And in it, hayom: this day, said about things that were already old.
Your line: this day, new. Today, do one familiar thing as if it were the first time you'd ever done it. Day five hundred fourteen.

515.title: Ki Tavo: coming in, going out (Deuteronomy 28:3–6)
515.hook: blessed in the city and the field, coming in and going out
515.tomorrow: Ki Tavo: a heart to know (Deuteronomy 29:3)
515.howItsDone: Some Jews touch the mezuzah on the doorframe when entering and leaving a home, and some say Psalm 121, with its line about going out and coming in, before a journey.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Ki Tavo, hayom: the old commandments, new each day. Your line was this day, new. What did you notice in something familiar? Today, blessings for every step of an ordinary day. Day five hundred fifteen.

Count how many thresholds you'll cross today. Out the front door. Into a car or onto a bus. Into work, or school, or a store. Back out. Back home. Most of those crossings take less than a second and leave no memory at all. On the doorframe of a Jewish home there's a small case, a mezuzah, and some people touch it as they pass, going in and going out. The doorway is treated as a place worth a moment. Today's verses bless exactly those crossings, and everything around them.
screen: `COUNT THE DOORWAYS.` → `A HAND ON THE MEZUZAH.` → `THE CROSSINGS, BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy twenty-eight opens with a list of blessings, if the people keep the covenant. It starts small and wide at the same time: "Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field." Then the children and the herds, the basket and the kneading-trough. And it ends: "Blessed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and blessed shalt thou be when thou goest out." City and field cover where you are. Coming in and going out cover how you move between them. Between the two, hardly a moment of the day is left out. The basket and the kneading-trough are kitchen things, where the bread begins. The blessing reaches right into the bowl. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, gives the last verse a second reading. Coming in and going out, it says, can mean coming into the world and leaving it: may your leaving be like your arriving, free of wrongdoing. A whole life read as one doorway. A psalm uses the same pair: "The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever." These blessings sit in a hard chapter. They're short, and the curses that follow are long and frightening; by custom the reader chants those quickly and in a lowered voice. But the chapter begins with blessing, and the blessing is about the plainest movements a person makes.
screen: `IN THE CITY, IN THE FIELD.` · `THE BASKET AND THE KNEADING-TROUGH.` · `ARRIVING IN, AND LEAVING, THE WORLD.` · `SHORT BLESSINGS, A HARD CHAPTER.` · then, large: `BLESSED COMING AND GOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless your leaving and your returning. Settle, and breathe. Picture the door you'll walk out of next. See your hand on it. Before you go through, imagine pausing for half a second. If you pray, the psalm's words are there: the LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in. If you don't, a breath and a wish that the day goes well will do. Now picture coming back through the same door tonight. Pause there too. Two thresholds, two small moments, kept. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. The portion where blessing covers the city and the field, the coming in and the going out.
Your line: blessed coming and going. Today, at one door, pause for a breath as you leave, and another as you come back. Day five hundred fifteen.

516.title: Ki Tavo: a heart to know (Deuteronomy 29:3)
516.hook: only after forty years are they given "a heart to know"
516.howItsDone: Jewish learning is traditionally lifelong: the same texts are studied again and again over decades, often with the same teacher or study partner, on the expectation that understanding deepens with age.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessings for the city and the field, for coming in and going out. Your line was blessed coming and going. Which door did you pause at? Today, a sentence about how long it takes to understand. Day five hundred sixteen.

A mother tells her fifteen-year-old something, and gets an eye-roll. Fifteen years later the daughter is standing in her own kitchen, and the sentence comes back, and this time it lands. It wasn't wrong back then. She just didn't have the heart for it yet. Near the end of Ki Tavo, Moses says something like this to a whole people. Forty years in, he tells them they're only now ready to understand.
screen: `AT FIFTEEN, AN EYE-ROLL.` → `AT THIRTY, IN THE KITCHEN.` → `ONLY NOW, A HEART FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Moses reminds them of everything they saw: the plagues in Egypt, the signs, the great wonders. And then: "But the LORD hath not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day." Forty years of wonders, and only now, at the edge of the river, a heart to know. In Hebrew, lev lada'at. In the Hebrew Bible the heart isn't mainly the seat of feelings. It's where a person thinks, understands and decides. A heart to know is a mind that can finally take it in. Rashi draws a lesson from the timing. He brings a teaching found in the Talmud: a student does not fully grasp the mind of a teacher until forty years have passed. The people have had Moses for forty years. Now, in his last days, they're ready to understand him. The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, has a list of the ages of a life, and one line says: at forty, understanding. Some things can't be hurried by effort. You can memorize a text in a week. Understanding it waits for the years that make it make sense. That isn't a failure of the student. It's how understanding works. Seeing comes first, and knowing can take years.
screen: `FORTY YEARS OF WONDERS.` · `LEV LADA'AT: A HEART TO KNOW.` · `FORTY YEARS TO GRASP A TEACHER.` · `AT FORTY, UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `UNDERSTANDING TAKES YEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with slow understanding. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you don't understand yet. A text that won't open, a person whose choices puzzle you, a part of your own life that hasn't made sense. Instead of pushing at it, set it down gently, like a seed in soil. You don't have to solve it in two minutes. Tell yourself it can take years, and that's allowed. Notice whatever shifts in your chest, if anything does. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. And lev lada'at, a heart to know, given only after forty years.
Your line: understanding takes years. Today, when something doesn't make sense yet, say to yourself: not yet, and that's fine. Day five hundred sixteen.

517.title: Nitzavim: all of you (Deuteronomy 29:9–10)
517.hook: everyone stands in the covenant, leaders and woodcutters and water-drawers alike
517.howItsDone: Nitzavim is read on the Shabbat before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes together with Vayelech, and its opening words, 'you are standing this day, all of you', are often taken up in sermons for the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a heart to know, given only after forty years. Your line was understanding takes years. What did you let be not yet? Today, a new portion, and a crowd. Day five hundred seventeen.

At any big gathering, a wedding, a graduation, a funeral, someone is at the front. Someone has the good seats. And someone is out back, in the kitchen, clearing plates, parking cars, carrying folding chairs. Nobody photographs them. Without them the day doesn't happen. The portion called Nitzavim opens with a crowd like that, and it does something unusual. It names the people in the kitchen. Not as an afterthought, and not at the edge. In the same sentence as the leaders.
screen: `THE FRONT, THE GOOD SEATS.` → `THE KITCHEN, THE PARKING LOT.` → `NAMED IN THE SAME SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Nitzavim means standing, standing firm. The portion opens: "Ye are standing this day all of you before the LORD your God: your heads, your tribes, your elders, and your officers, even all the men of Israel." Then the list keeps going: the little ones, the wives, the stranger in the camp, "from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water." That's the whole society, top to bottom. All of you. Elsewhere in the Bible, in the book of Joshua, cutting wood and drawing water is the work given to outsiders with little standing. The people who did it didn't make decisions. They made the fire and the water possible. And here they stand in the covenant, named, no lower in the sentence's dignity than anyone else. Rashi, following a midrash, says these woodcutters and water-drawers were people from outside who had come to join Israel. If so, the circle is wider still: newcomers stand in the covenant too. It matters when this portion is read: on the Shabbat just before Rosh Hashanah, sometimes paired with the next portion, as the season of standing in judgment arrives. The text, read that week, puts everyone in the same line. No one stands alone, and no one is ranked. In a synagogue, the people who set out chairs, cook for the meal afterward, and lock up at night are the reason anyone else can be there at all. Nitzavim gives them their own line.
screen: `NITZAVIM: STANDING.` · `HEADS, ELDERS, OFFICERS.` · `THE HEWER OF WOOD, THE DRAWER OF WATER.` · `EVERYONE STANDS, UNRANKED.` · then, large: `ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: value one role people overlook. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you spend time: work, school, a building, a congregation, your own home. Who makes it work without being seen? The cleaner, the night guard, the person who restocks the shelves, the one who always notices when the dish soap runs out. See their face if you can. Let them stand, in your mind, in the same line as the people at the front. Then think of one small way to tell them you've noticed. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. The portion where everyone stands together, from the heads of the tribes to the drawer of water.
Your line: all of you. Today, thank one person whose work usually goes unseen, by name if you can. Day five hundred seventeen.

518.title: Nitzavim: those not here today (Deuteronomy 29:13–14)
518.hook: the covenant includes "him that is not here with us this day"
518.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often cite this verse to explain why each generation counts itself part of the covenant, and why converts to Judaism are traditionally described as having been present when it was made.

segments.voice: Yesterday, everyone standing together, from the leaders to the water-drawers. Your line was all of you. Whose unseen work did you thank? Today, the people who weren't in the crowd at all. Day five hundred eighteen.

People do strange, hopeful things for strangers in the future. They bury time capsules with letters to readers not yet born. They write wills. They plant oak trees that won't give real shade for decades. A town council approves a bridge that will outlast every person in the room. Moses, standing before the whole camp on the plains of Moab, does something stranger than any of these. He makes a covenant binding on people who aren't there.
screen: `A TIME CAPSULE.` → `AN OAK FOR SOMEONE ELSE'S SHADE.` → `A COVENANT WITH THE ABSENT.`

segments.voice: "Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath; but with him that standeth here with us this day before the LORD our God, and also with him that is not here with us this day." Who isn't there? The plain reading: future generations. Children not yet born, and their children after them. The Talmud, in Shevuot, reads it to include the generations to come and those who would one day join the Jewish people as converts. The midrash goes further: the souls of all those generations were somehow present at that moment, standing in the covenant. That's why a convert is sometimes described as a soul that was already there, coming home. Read it as mysticism or as poetry; either way the idea is plain. A covenant isn't only a contract between people in the same room. It reaches forward. The people standing that day are holding something on behalf of people they'll never meet. And every generation since has been, in a sense, the ones who were not here, now arrived. This week ran through Ki Tavo and into Nitzavim. The first goes to thanks. A wandering father. This day, new. Blessed coming and going. Understanding takes years. All of you. And today, those not yet here. A week that began with the farmer remembering his past, and ends with people far in the future.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of generations to come. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone who'll be alive a hundred years from now. Maybe a great-grandchild. Maybe a stranger who'll live in your town, walk your street, read the books you read. You'll never meet them. What would you want to hand them? A habit, a story, a cleaner river, a kinder way of arguing? Choose one small thing you're doing now that they might someday stand on. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. Including the ones who weren't yet standing anywhere.
Your line: those not yet here. Today, do one thing whose good will outlast you, even a small one. Day five hundred eighteen.
